title: Rasuwa Flood Response: Drone Relief with WFP
description: Field leadership, drone mapping and data processing, and cargo-drone piloting with UN WFP after the Rasuwa flood, supporting rescue, relief distribution, and communication across the river.
fullText:
After the Bhotekoshi flood hit Rasuwa, our Airlift team worked with the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) to get supplies across disrupted routes. We used cargo drones for deliveries, the M4E for preliminary mapping, and a drone-mounted speaker to communicate with villagers across the river.

I led the field team, coordinated directly with WFP, and piloted the FlyCart 100 and FlyCart 30. I also carried out drone mapping and data processing, delivering orthomosaics, DSMs, and 3D models during the early flood response to support rescue and relief distribution.

### How we worked

1. **Assess the area:** visit potential operating sites and use M4E preliminary mapping to understand the terrain.
2. **Coordinate on the ground:** work with WFP and the field team around supplies, operating locations, and approvals.
3. **Reach across the river:** use the drone-mounted speaker to speak with villagers where communication links were disrupted.
4. **Fly essential supplies:** operate the FlyCart 100 and FlyCart 30 to move relief goods across disrupted routes.

![A river winding through a steep green valley, with buildings and a hillside road below.](/images/rasuwa/river-valley.webp)

## The flood that cut communities off

On 26 August 2026, flooding along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers devastated parts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading. Homes, roads, bridges, and livelihoods were lost. Steep terrain and monsoon conditions made access even harder. [UN Nepal's account of the response](https://nepal.un.org/en/323295-one-month-rasuwa-floods-six-ways-coordinated-action-making-difference).

Relief supplies had to reach people while normal transport and communication links were still disrupted.

## Early mapping for rescue and relief

In the first days of the flood response, I carried out drone mapping and processed the collected data into orthomosaics, digital surface models (DSMs), and 3D models. I delivered these outputs early in the response to support rescue and relief-distribution operations in the community.

This gave our work a geospatial role alongside cargo delivery. The processed data helped the people organising rescue and relief understand the affected area and plan their work.

### What I delivered

- **Orthomosaics:** a stitched aerial view of the mapped area for an overview of the ground situation.
- **Digital surface models:** surface-elevation data representing the terrain and features above it.
- **3D models:** a three-dimensional representation of the mapped area.
- **Early operational support:** processed mapping outputs made available during the first days of the response for rescue and relief distribution.

## Finding where we could operate

We left Kathmandu for Bidur on 4 September and continued to Briddhim the next day for initial food-delivery flights. An inauguration programme and another delivery followed on 6 September.

From Dhunche, we assessed Thulo Syafru, Ramche, and Karmi Danda and carried out preliminary mapping with the M4E. We needed workable locations on the ground before establishing a delivery route.

By 10 September, we had selected the route from Thulo Bharkhu to Gre village. Flights began that afternoon and continued the next day.

## Where the road ended

I also visited the Chilime hydropower tunnel area. At the time, it was the last point we could reach by vehicle along that route. Beyond it, flood damage had cut off normal access.

Seeing the destruction around Syafrubesi was difficult to take in. I had always admired our mountains and rivers. Now, the same landscape held the loss of homes, familiar places, and people. I struggled to reconcile that beauty with the devastation before me.

I kept thinking about children waiting for parents who would never return. We could bring food and medicine, but we could not bring a parent home. I worried about who would care for them and how they would find security again. That grief stayed with me as we worked.

![A rocky river channel with muddy water between steep slopes.](/images/rasuwa/river-channel.webp)

## Managing the team and flying the deliveries

My role connected field management with the flights themselves. I coordinated with WFP, organised the team, and piloted the cargo drones. Each day's work depended on the operating location, available supplies, and permission to proceed.

Our Gre deliveries included rice, lentils, oil, and salt. We also coordinated with the district administration, meeting the Deputy Chief District Officer on 11 September and continuing discussions in the following days.

### My responsibilities in the field

- **Team management:** organise the field team and handle day-to-day work on site.
- **Client coordination:** stay in direct contact with UN WFP about the operation.
- **Flight operations:** pilot the FlyCart 100 and FlyCart 30 for cargo deliveries.
- **Local coordination:** take part in discussions with the district administration about continuing operations.

![Two people working together on a cargo drone beside a road.](/images/rasuwa/aircraft-preparation.webp)

## Speaking to villagers across the river

With communication links disrupted, we used a speaker attached to a drone to speak with villagers on the other side of the river.

Carrying our voices across that gap made the aircraft's capabilities feel very real to me. The drone could help us communicate with people we could not readily reach, as well as carry the goods they needed.

### The tools behind the response

- **Drone-mounted speaker:** carry our voices to villagers across the river when normal communication links were disrupted.
- **FlyCart 100 and FlyCart 30:** transport essential goods during the relief operation.
- **M4E preliminary mapping:** support assessment of the area before delivery operations.
- **Field coordination:** bring the team, WFP, operating locations, and available supplies together on the ground.

![A person holding a drone controller against a mountain backdrop.](/images/rasuwa/flight-controller.webp)

## A namaste I will remember

During the operation, elderly villagers around my grandparents' age came to me with tears in their eyes and greeted me with a namaste. They were happy to see our team helping people who were going hungry.

Their greeting moved me deeply. I thought of my own grandparents and how vulnerable it must feel to depend on others for food after losing access to so much. I felt grateful that we could help, and responsible for keeping the work going carefully.

Their faces and folded hands are what I remember most clearly from Rasuwa.

![Shradaya Raj Poudel wearing a WFP vest beside an older community member carrying a sack.](/images/rasuwa/community-and-field-team.webp)

*With a community member during the relief operation.*

## The days when flights had to wait

On 12 September, we were waiting for supplies when the operation was placed on hold following discussions involving WFP and the district administration.

We assessed the Syafrubesi area on 13 September. Discussions about aviation and district-level approval continued, and by 16 September the team remained grounded. During those pauses, I kept the team coordinated and stayed in contact with WFP about the next stage.

## Deliveries to Dadagaun

Between 19 and 22 September, we operated from Bimire in Uttargaya-04 to Dadagaun in Uttargaya-02.

Alongside rice, we carried medicines, electrolyte powder, vitamins, and nutritional supplements. On 22 September, deliveries also included sanitary pads and baby diapers. The work addressed a range of everyday needs beyond staple food.

### What we carried

- **Staple food:** rice, alongside the lentils, oil, and salt carried during the earlier Gre operations.
- **Health supplies:** medicines, electrolyte powder, and vitamins.
- **Nutrition support:** nutritional supplements included in the delivery records.
- **Personal care:** sanitary pads and baby diapers carried on 22 September.

![Bags of supplies and people gathered near a helicopter in misty conditions.](/images/rasuwa/supplies-at-operating-site.webp)

## What coordination made possible

Our team was part of a wider effort involving the Government of Nepal, Nepal Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, NGOs, international organisations, and private companies. In the field, I saw how much depended on bringing those efforts together.

The response also received international attention. WFP described this as its first emergency deployment of humanitarian cargo drones and discussed how the experience could inform operations elsewhere. I felt proud to contribute to that work. [Read WFP's account](https://www.wfp.org/stories/nepal-floods-where-roads-stop-humanitarian-cargo-drones-deliver).

### How responsibilities connected

- **WFP:** our client and direct coordination point for the delivery project.
- **District administration:** discussions concerning permission and the continuation of operations.
- **Airlift field team:** assessment, preparation, piloting, and delivery work on site.
- **Wider response:** government, security forces, humanitarian organisations, and private companies contributing to relief.

![Field team member alongside WFP’s Country Director for Nepal, standing behind a cargo drone with a helicopter in the background.](/images/rasuwa/response-team-and-aircraft.webp)

*With WFP’s Country Director for Nepal in the field.*

## Leaving the operation ready to continue

Before returning to Kathmandu, I arranged for the operation to continue with other team members. By that point, our team had supplied 5,000 kg of goods to people in Rasuwa.

Teammates continued for another week after I left. The response extended beyond my own time in the field, and its achievements belonged to the whole team.

### Continuity beyond my deployment

1. **Before returning:** I made the arrangements needed for other team members to continue the operation.
2. **At my return:** our team had supplied 5,000 kg of goods; this was the milestone reached before I left.
3. **The following week:** teammates continued the project after I returned to Kathmandu.

![A field team member holding a handheld radio, with a drone and cargo container behind him.](/images/rasuwa/field-portrait.webp)

## The difference our work made

- **5,000 kg supplied:** our team's delivery milestone before I returned to Kathmandu.
- **Essential goods across disrupted routes:** food, medicine, nutritional and hygiene supplies moved on the Thulo Bharkhu to Gre and Bimire to Dadagaun routes.
- **Mapping for rescue and relief:** I delivered orthomosaics, DSMs, and 3D models in the early response to support community rescue and relief-distribution operations.
- **Communication across the river:** a drone-mounted speaker let us speak with villagers whose usual communication links were disrupted.
- **Another week of operations:** after I arranged continuation and returned to Kathmandu, teammates carried the work forward.

These deliveries met immediate needs while the wider work of restoring access, services, and security for families continued.

## What I took from Rasuwa

I came home proud of our team and sad for everything people had lost. I remember supplies lifting into the air, our voices reaching across the river, and elderly villagers greeting me with tearful eyes and folded hands.

Those memories belong together. We could offer practical help in a terrible moment, and I am grateful I could be there to do my part.
dataPointsRaw:
Supplied before my return: 5,000 kg
Client: UN WFP
Cargo aircraft: FlyCart 100 / 30
Preliminary mapping: M4E
